summary: Adds a per-key token bucket in front of every public API route: 60 requests a minute, then 429 with Retry-After.

questions.question: Why a token bucket here, instead of counting requests in a fixed one-minute window?
questions.rubric:
- A fixed window lets a client send up to twice the limit across a window boundary.
- The bucket refills continuously: bursts up to the limit, but the average rate holds.
- Refill is computed when a request arrives, so there is no timer or cleanup job.

rules.feedback: Right: a fixed window allows a double burst at the boundary, and the bucket keeps the average.
Bursts, yes. Missing: why a fixed window is worse at its boundary.
Simpler than what? Name the alternative and what it gets wrong.

default.feedback: Nothing here shows the developer could defend this part.

questions.question: A client sends every request with a new, made-up api_key. What happens to this server?
questions.rubric:
- Every new key starts with a full bucket, so the limit never applies.
- _buckets gains an entry per key and is never cleaned, so memory grows until the process falls over.
- Fix: reject unknown keys before limiting, limit per IP as well, or bound the map.

rules.feedback: Exactly: no limit for new keys, and _buckets grows without bound. Reject unknown keys first.
New keys bypass the limit, yes. Missing: the dict grows forever, which is the outage.
This is about keys nobody issued, not the normal rate.

default.feedback: Nothing here shows the developer could defend this part.

questions.question: Why a plain dict of (tokens, last refill) per key, and what does that choice cost?
questions.rubric:
- Constant-time lookup and update, no dependency, two numbers per key.
- It lives in one process: not shared between workers or servers, lost on restart.
- Nothing ever removes an entry.

rules.feedback: Right about per-process. Missing: entries are never removed.
Fast, yes. Missing what it costs: per process, and never evicted.

default.feedback: Nothing here shows the developer could defend this part.

questions.question: Where does this limit stop holding?
questions.rubric:
- Several workers or servers each keep their own buckets, so a key gets that many times the limit.
- A restart or deploy refills every bucket.
- Concurrent requests can both spend the last token.

rules.feedback: Yes: N servers give N times the limit, and a deploy resets every bucket.
Restarts, yes. Missing: several servers each keep their own buckets.

default.feedback: Nothing here shows the developer could defend this part.

questions.question: How would you show the 61st request in a minute gets a 429, without waiting a minute?
questions.rubric:
- Call _allow with explicit times instead of the real clock.
- 61 calls at the same instant: 60 allowed, the 61st refused.
- Retry-After is about one second, and a call one second later is allowed.

rules.feedback: Good: drive _allow with explicit times, assert the 61st is refused and the Retry-After.
Sleeping a minute in a test is slow and flaky. Pass the time in instead.

default.feedback: Nothing here shows the developer could defend this part.
